ruminate about how to get even with assailant

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't deal with even the slightest upset
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
I have failed in my most important role in life

vignette: Arthur Vance was seventy-one when the silence finally grew too loud to bear, but the fracture had happened twenty years earlier during his shift at the downtown transit hub. He remembered the morning routine: the smell of stale coffee, the weight of his radio, the quiet rhythm of scanning passengers. Then the blast. It was a sudden, violent concussion that knocked the breath from his lungs and turned the marble floor into shrapnel. In the chaos, Arthur had frozen. He could not move his arms to direct the panicked crowd, could not speak over the roaring collapse of the ceiling. When the smoke cleared, three strangers were dead. He had walked away with only a bruised rib, but the guilt was a heavier wound. Now, twenty years later, the memory refused to settle. Some mornings, the footage played in hyper-clarity in his mind—the exact shade of a man’s coat before he fell, the precise crack of the glass, the smell of burnt insulation. He could recount every second, yet he had never managed to piece it into a coherent narrative that made sense to himself. Other times, he would sit at his kitchen table and describe the event in flat, detached tones, feeling absolutely nothing, as if reading about a stranger’s misfortune. His conviction that he had failed his most important duty, combined with the belief that he lacked the fortitude to cope and that others would have handled the crisis far better, directly drove his survival strategies. He began scanning every face that approached his security checkpoint with exhausting scrutiny, hunting for any hint of menace, and he stopped going out once the sun went down. At his desk, he could not bear to face the room, so he always positioned his chair with his back pressed firmly against the heavy concrete wall, forcing his eyes to track every movement across the lobby. When his shift ended, the quiet of his apartment became a canvas for his frustration, and he would lie awake replaying the attack, fixated on the exact moment he could have intervened, nursing a quiet, unshakable urge to make the perpetrators pay. Yet the very act of constantly monitoring for danger and barricading himself against the room only served to fracture his recollection of the past. His rigid posturing and obsessive scrutiny prevented his mind from integrating the experience, leaving the memories raw and vividly intact while simultaneously draining them of any emotional context. This emotional numbness and the relentless mental loop then confirmed his original fears: he told himself that such a disjointed response proved he could never cope, and that his inability to form a clear account of what happened only reinforced his conviction that he was fundamentally broken compared to his peers. Over the years, the habits calcified. His wife noticed how he flinched at the sound of a car backfiring outside their house, how he would suddenly stand and check the locks three times before allowing her to sit beside him. At his current post at a suburban business park, the environment itself became a minefield. A dropped metal crate in the parking lot sent him vaulting over his console, while a delivery driver walking too quickly toward his gate triggered the same paralyzing assessment of danger that had frozen him decades ago. He was working less, taking early leave when his hands shook too badly to operate the gate controls, and the shame of his withdrawal was mounting. What finally brought Arthur to my office was the quiet admission that he could no longer sit through his own retirement dinner. He was terrified that the numbness was spreading to his marriage, and he was hoping, against his own better judgment, that someone might help him untangle the knot he had been pulling tighter for twenty years.
